blocks.text: Bound how long a caller waits for an operation, so a slow dependency cannot hold its threads and its own callers hostage.

Every remote call needs an upper bound, because a hung call holds a thread, a connection and a user. Per-call timeouts are not enough: a request that makes five calls needs one **deadline** for the whole request, and each call gets what is left of it.

items: **Connect timeout:** how long to establish the connection; usually short.
**Read (socket) timeout:** the longest gap without data, not the total time.
**Deadline:** an absolute point in time, propagated downstream.

blocks.text: A timeout abandons the wait, not the work. The remote side may still complete, so a timed-out write has an unknown outcome.

walkthrough.note: A deadline is an absolute instant read from an injected `Clock`. `remaining()` is what the request may still spend.
A scripted fake: if its latency exceeds the timeout it burns exactly the timeout on the fake clock and fails, otherwise it burns its latency.
Each call receives `cap(perCall)`: the smaller of its own limit and the remaining budget. No call can outlive the request.
A 300 ms budget: auth leaves 260, stock leaves 140, price is capped at 140 ms rather than its own 250 ms, and audit fails fast without calling.

blocks.text: A checkout page that fans out to four services.

The gateway promises the browser a response within two seconds. It calls pricing, stock, loyalty and fraud in sequence. Without a shared deadline, four calls with a 1.5 s limit each can take six seconds, long after the browser gave up. The gateway stamps a deadline on the request and every outbound call carries the remaining budget, in gRPC as the deadline itself.

blocks.text: Payoff: worst-case latency is the budget, and work for a caller that has already left is never started.

lists.title: Use when
items: Any call crosses a process or network boundary.
A request fans out and must answer within a promised latency.
A slow dependency is worse than a failed one.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The operation is a local, bounded computation.
Cancelling mid-way leaves a non-idempotent write in an unknown state.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: No timeout at all: many default clients wait forever.
Stacked timeouts where the inner exceeds the outer, so the inner never fires first.
Retrying a timed-out call that is not idempotent.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: One global 30 s timeout copied everywhere regardless of real latency.
Timeouts so tight that normal tail latency trips them constantly.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: `StructuredTaskScope.joinUntil(Instant)` applies one deadline to a whole group of subtasks (preview API).

rows.difference: A timeout turns an unbounded wait into a failure; a retry decides what to do with that failure. Each attempt needs its own timeout inside the overall deadline.
Timeouts are the failures a breaker counts. The timeout bounds one call; the breaker stops making calls once timeouts pile up.
A bulkhead limits how many calls run at once; a timeout limits how long one call may run. Without timeouts, a bulkhead's permits are held forever.
A rate limiter bounds how often requests start. A timeout bounds how long each one may take.

entries.detail: Completes the future exceptionally with `TimeoutException` after the given delay.

entries.detail: Waits at most the given time and throws `TimeoutException`; the task itself keeps running unless cancelled.

entries.name: Deadline
entries.detail: `io.grpc.Deadline` is an absolute point in time that is propagated to servers and downstream calls.

entries.name: TimeLimiter
entries.detail: Wraps a `Future` or `CompletionStage` and fails it with `TimeoutException` after the configured duration.

exercises.prompt: Explain why per-call timeouts are not enough, and what a timeout does not do.

modelAnswer.text: Sequential calls each within their own limit can add up to far more than the caller will wait, so the request needs one deadline that every call is capped by. A timeout only stops waiting; the remote work may still finish, so a timed-out write has an unknown outcome and needs idempotency before any retry.

keyPoints: Every remote call needs an upper bound
One request deadline, with each call capped by the remaining budget
Connect, read and total time are different limits
A timeout abandons the wait, not the remote work
